Field surveys of Yellowing flyingfish (Cypselurus poecilopterus) in the warm waters of the tropical Pacific have provided detailed life-history parameters for this epipelagic species. The maximum recorded fork length, a widely used metric for size in flyingfishes, reaches 27.0 centimeters [Li = 27.0 centimeters], a value that places this species among the moderately sized members of the Exocoetidae. Early developmental stages are remarkably brief; the incubation period for externally fertilised eggs, which are pelagic and possess a transparent chorion, lasts approximately 2 days [ab = approximately 2 days] when maintained at a stable water temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. Upon eclosion, the newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic and possess a modest wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], reflecting the small initial size typical of exocoetid eggs. This rapid hatching interval is consistent with the energetic strategy of minimising the vulnerable egg stage in the open ocean, where predation pressure on sessile or drifting embryos is intense.

As the yolk-sac larva transitions to an exogenously feeding, actively growing larva, growth trajectories become highly dependent on local thermal conditions. Based on the size-corrected growth model for the genus, and under the consistent thermal regime of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C] that characterises its subtropical nursery grounds, the fork length at puberty is estimated at 18.8 centimeters [Lp = 18.8 centimeters]. This length marks the onset of gonadal maturation and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis in this species. The time since birth at this developmental milestone, derived from von Bertalanffy growth curves fitted to length-at-age data, is 170 days since birth [tp = 170 days since birth] at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This relatively protracted juvenile phase likely reflects the need for substantial somatic investment before the first reproductive event, allowing individuals to attain the size necessary for the energetically expensive gliding flight and spawning aggregations that characterise adult life.

Reproductive output in Yellowing flyingfish is tightly coupled to body size and ambient temperature, with females typically spawning multiple batches of pelagic eggs over an extended breeding season. A mature female can achieve a maximum daily reproductive rate of 30 eggs per day [Ri = 30 eggs per day] under optimal conditions at 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C], a figure derived from size-corrected fecundity estimates for the closely related Hirundichthys affinis. This high egg production rate, sustained by iteroparous spawning events, is a critical life-history adaptation that offsets the considerable larval mortality experienced during the planktonic phase. When expressed in more conventional terms, this translates to approximately 30 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 30 eggs per spawning event] with a rapid turnover of successive clutches. The energetic costs of such sustained gamete production likely constrain adult body condition and foraging behaviour during the reproductive season.

Lifespan data for this species are limited, but the maximum documented longevity under natural conditions is 547.5 days [am = 547.5 days], again recorded at the species' typical thermal environment of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This relatively short lifespan, equivalent to approximately one and a half years, is characteristic of many small-to-medium pelagic teleosts, which face high natural mortality from predation by tunas, billfishes, and seabirds. The resulting life-history strategy is one of early and intense reproduction, with individuals reaching the end of their natural lifespan shortly after completing their primary reproductive contributions. Senescence in this species is poorly documented, but post-spawning mortality likely increases sharply as body condition deteriorates following the sustained energetic investment in spawning aggregations.

Comparative analysis with other exocoetid species reveals interesting patterns in size and reproductive scaling. The ultimate fork length of 27.0 centimeters [Li = 27.0 centimeters] observed in Cypselurus poecilopterus is notably smaller than the maximum sizes reported for larger members of the genus Cypselurus, which may exceed 35 centimeters. This relatively modest body size is consistent with the reduced time to puberty, here estimated at 170 days following hatching [tp = 170 days following hatching], as smaller-bodied species tend to mature more rapidly at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. The trade-off between attaining a larger asymptotic size and the energetic demands of prolonged somatic growth is evident; by investing less in continued growth after maturity, this species allocates a substantial fraction of assimilated resources to the high daily egg output of 30 eggs per day [Ri = 30 eggs per day] during its brief adult phase. This strategy aligns with predictions for a short-lived, rapidly maturing pelagic fish subject to heavy predation throughout its life cycle.
